13F reports cover LONG positions in Section 13(f) securities (US exchange-traded equities plus reportable options, warrants, certain convertibles) held by managers with at least $100M in such securities — so managers below that threshold are absent entirely. No short positions, no cash, no non-13(f) assets — not a full portfolio, and not a census of institutional ownership.

Positions are quarter-end snapshots filed up to 45 days late — not current holdings. A position may have been changed or closed before you ever see it, and is older still by however long ago that quarter ended.

Values are the manager's stated market value at quarter-end in era-dependent units (whole dollars for form versions effective 2023-01-03 onward, thousands before), normalized here to whole dollars with unit_basis carried on every record.

Affiliated managers may report the same position (otherManager), so one position can appear under more than one filer.

Positions under confidential treatment may be omitted until a later amendment discloses them.

These are disclosures, not investment advice (ARCHITECTURE.md §5.2 / M2-CONTRACT §5).

signalsRankingHtml:
How signal rows are ranked (triage v1.0.0)

A signal is a fact about a filing, not a forecast: no returns are computed, and no price, return or intent is read. "Filings to read" on /signals classifies each filing that carries an active signal against the filer's own record, by published rules; it does not predict anything.

  • Rows. Filings filed inside the 90-day window that carry at least one active signal on a listed-stock line (options excluded). Grouped in this order: a late batch (one member's filings on one date that complete 2 or more co-occurrence clusters whose windows ended before the window opened); a cluster (an active co-occurrence, absorbing every filing in its window whose lead line is that ticker and side); same member and ticker (filings whose lead lines share a ticker, as "N filings"); and the single filing.
  • Point in time. Every meter is computed at a cutoff and sees only rows filed on or before it: a single filing at its filed date; each filing of a same-member-and-ticker row at its own filed date; a cluster at its latest absorbed filing; a late batch at its date.
  • Size — the lower bound against the filer's prior disclosures. Strong: at least one bracket above the largest of the filer's prior disclosures and a lower bound of $50,001 or more. Medium: a bracket above, or the same bracket at $50,001 or more. Low: at least $15,001 and above 90% of the prior lower bounds. Unknown with fewer than 5 prior disclosures that state one. Prior means traded earlier, in another filing, and filed by this row's cutoff.
  • Pattern — the gap since the filer's previous trade. Strong: the first filing on record, or 730 days or more since the previous trade. Medium: 365 days or more. Low: 180 days or more. Measured from the filing's earliest trade date over rows filed by the cutoff.
  • Others — members disclosing the same ticker and side in one co-occurrence window. Strong: 5 or more distinct members in the active co-occurrence window that holds the trade; medium: 4. Only filings filed by the cutoff are counted, so a member who filed later never raises an earlier filing.
  • Cmte — the issuer inside a committee the member sat on at the trade date. Medium: a direct match — the issuer's 4-digit SIC inside a direct range of a committee that matched (table v1 on Methodology). Low: a sector match only. None: no mapped committee matched. Unknown: the sector or the membership on that date is not on record, or the committee inputs are not in this build. The overlap is context, never an allegation — it states a sector-to-committee fact and nothing about intent.
  • Brackets. The floors of the statutory ranges: $1,001, $15,001, $50,001, $100,001, $250,001, $500,001, $1,000,001, $5,000,001, $25,000,001, $50,000,001.
  • Tiers. A row led by an exchange is Routine. Otherwise any meter at strong is Stands out; any at medium, or a sum of 3 or more over the meters that are known, is Worth a look; the rest are Routine. Lateness is a tag, never a ranking input.
  • Lead line and order. A row's meter is the strongest over its lines. Its lead line has the strongest meter, then the highest sum, then is not an exchange, then has the highest lower bound. Stands out and Worth a look sort by the count of strong meters, the sum, the lead lower bound and the filed date; Routine by filed date.
  • Reason sentence. Generated from the row's facts by fixed templates, without pronouns, at most 160 characters.
  • Lead cards. From the ranked listed-stock lines. Committee: direct matches before broad, then the lower bound, then the filed date. Largest buy and sell, own record: filers with at least 20 prior disclosures spanning 365 days or more, lines of at least $50,001, ranked by brackets above the filer's largest prior disclosure; absolute: by lower bound, then filed date.

A 13F is a quarterly, long-only snapshot filed up to 45 days late — not current holdings. what a 13F covers ↗

13F reports cover LONG positions in Section 13(f) securities (US exchange-traded equities plus reportable options, warrants, certain convertibles) held by managers with at least $100M in such securities — so managers below that threshold are absent entirely. No short positions, no cash, no non-13(f) assets — not a full portfolio, and not a census of institutional ownership.

Positions are quarter-end snapshots filed up to 45 days late — not current holdings. A position may have been changed or closed before you ever see it, and is older still by however long ago that quarter ended.

Values are the manager's stated market value at quarter-end in era-dependent units (whole dollars for form versions effective 2023-01-03 onward, thousands before), normalized here to whole dollars with unit_basis carried on every record.

Affiliated managers may report the same position (otherManager), so one position can appear under more than one filer.

Positions under confidential treatment may be omitted until a later amendment discloses them.

These are disclosures, not investment advice (ARCHITECTURE.md §5.2 / M2-CONTRACT §5).

Opportunistic member buy

OPP. BUYRule A listed-stock purchase in Filings to read by a member who traded in each of the 3 prior years but never in one fixed month each year (the CMP routine test). Members with under 3 years of history are unclassified. Broad accounts (more than 25 names in the 90 days before the trade) are left out.The routine test is the site's adaptation of Cohen, Malloy & Pomorski's, whose sample is corporate insiders. The rule ↗Horizon CMP: portfolios formed monthly on the filing. The Congress studies: one month to a year.

Strip out routine traders — people who trade in the same calendar month year after year, for pay or liquidity — and what is left carries the information. Proven for corporate insiders; adapted here to members of Congress.

Split. The routine filter is proven for corporate insiders and untested on Congress; studies after the STOCK Act find no average edge for member purchases.

Opportunistic insider purchases

INSIDERRule Proposed: open-market purchases (Form 4 code P) by insiders not tagged routine; routine = traded in the same calendar month in each of the 3 prior years. Extra weight when 2 or more insiders of one issuer buy within 30 days — a proposed refinement, not tested in the paper.Horizon Portfolios formed monthly on the filing.

Over half of corporate insider trades are routine — made in the same calendar month for years, for pay or liquidity — and carry no information. Strip them out and what is left is informed money.

A 13F is a quarterly, long-only snapshot filed up to 45 days late — not current holdings. what a 13F covers ↗

13F reports cover LONG positions in Section 13(f) securities (US exchange-traded equities plus reportable options, warrants, certain convertibles) held by managers with at least $100M in such securities — so managers below that threshold are absent entirely. No short positions, no cash, no non-13(f) assets — not a full portfolio, and not a census of institutional ownership.

Positions are quarter-end snapshots filed up to 45 days late — not current holdings. A position may have been changed or closed before you ever see it, and is older still by however long ago that quarter ended.

Values are the manager's stated market value at quarter-end in era-dependent units (whole dollars for form versions effective 2023-01-03 onward, thousands before), normalized here to whole dollars with unit_basis carried on every record.

Affiliated managers may report the same position (otherManager), so one position can appear under more than one filer.

Positions under confidential treatment may be omitted until a later amendment discloses them.

These are disclosures, not investment advice (ARCHITECTURE.md §5.2 / M2-CONTRACT §5).

Overlap: Congress and notable managers on one name

The Overlap tab on /signals lists the names that members of Congress traded and notable managers changed in the same 13F quarter. It is a co-occurrence in public filings — never coordination, never intent — and it computes no price and no return.

  • The join. The same quarter join as the Congress column (above): Congress lines by trade date inside the quarter, listed stock as filed, a ticker, a purchase or a sale; 13F changes by the quarter they report. Tickers compare in the SEC spelling, so a name filed under a different spelling on the two sides is not matched.
  • Counts. Congress: the distinct members with a purchase line (▲) and with a sale line (▼) on the name. Notable managers: the distinct managers with a new stake or an add (▲), and with a trim or an exit (▼).
  • Direction. Each side's net: the larger of its two counts, or mixed on a tie. The relation is same when the two directions agree, opposite when they differ, and mixed when either side is mixed. A name is unanimous when neither side is split.
  • Order. Same, then opposite, then mixed; unanimous names first; then the larger Congress count plus the larger manager count, highest first; then the ticker.
  • Broad accounts. A member who traded more than 25 distinct tickers in the quarter matches almost any name, so the default view does not count them, and a name only they traded is not listed. "Broad accounts" counts them; an opened row lists their lines apart in either view.
  • Detail. An opened row lists at most 12 Congress lines a side, each with its range, owner, both dates and its receipt, the rest on the ticker page; and each manager's largest change on the name, at most 5 managers a side, each with its 13F receipt.
  • What the page carries. In each view (the two variants, each by All, Same and Opposite) the first 24 names — 12 when the page would pass its byte budget — and 12 show before "Show 12 more". Every count is the true total; where a view runs past what the page carries, the tab says so.

Playbooks: published research on the patterns the rows show

The Playbooks tab on /signals names published research on a pattern a row shows and quotes what it found, with evidence on both sides. The numbers are the papers' own, from their samples and years. Public Filings reads no price and computes no return, so it cannot say whether a pattern still holds; nothing here is advice.

  • Opportunistic member buy — the rule, adapted. Cohen, Malloy & Pomorski's routine test is for corporate insiders; the site adapts it to members of Congress. It applies to a row that is not a cluster and whose lead line is a listed-stock purchase with a ticker and a trade date. Of the member's rows without a date anomaly (any asset, any side) traded before the lead's year and filed by the row's cutoff, the member is unclassified without a trade in each of the 3 prior calendar years, routine when one calendar month has a trade in all 3, and opportunistic otherwise. It triggers on an opportunistic member who traded at most 25 distinct tickers in the 90 days before the trade (filed by the cutoff).
  • Leadership trade. It triggers when any ranked line of a row is by a member who held one of the 12 posts of Wei & Zhou (2025), NBER Working Paper 34524, Table A1 on the line's trade date (the roster below: from its start date, inclusive, to its end, exclusive). The roster (v1) starts 2023-01-03: a trade before it is never classified. The Speakers are dated to the day; the other posts by Congress or by year, as the official lists give them, starting or ending on the first day of a Congress (2023-01-03, 2025-01-03).
  • Committee-linked trade. It triggers when a row's Cmte meter reads medium — a direct match in the committee table (above). When the committee inputs are not in a build it has no rows, and the tab says it is unavailable. The overlap is context, never an allegation — it states a sector-to-committee fact and nothing about intent.
  • Best ideas and Consensus trigger on panels, not rows: the new-position leaders and Consensus on the Institutional tab state how many managers and names qualify. Opportunistic insider purchases need Form 4 data Public Filings does not hold.

  • Best ideas (Institutional · Live · evidence supportive). A notable manager’s largest new position at 2% or more of its 13F long book (Conviction leaders). Horizon studied: Monthly returns after the quarter’s holdings are known. Sources: Supports — Cohen, Polk & Silli (2010); later Antón, Cohen & Polk, “Best Ideas”, LSE working paper (US mutual funds, 1991–2005), personal.lse.ac.uk/polk/research/BestIdeas.pdf ↗.
  • Notable-manager consensus (Institutional · Live · evidence weak). Three or more notable managers moved the same name in the closed quarter (Consensus). Horizon studied: Quarterly holdings. Sources: Indirect — Cohen, Coval & Pástor (2005), Journal of Finance 60(3) (US equity funds), www.nber.org/papers/w9359 ↗; Against — Griffin & Xu (2009), Review of Financial Studies 22(7) (13F holdings, 1986–2004), ideas.repec.org/a/oup/rfinst/v22y2009i7p2331-2370.html ↗.
  • Congress and managers on one name (Overlap · Descriptive · evidence no studies). The Overlap tab’s rule. Horizon studied: — No published study found.
  • Opportunistic insider purchases (Form 4 · Needs Form 4 · evidence needs data). Proposed: open-market purchases (Form 4 code P) by insiders not tagged routine; routine = traded in the same calendar month in each of the 3 prior years. Extra weight when 2 or more insiders of one issuer buy within 30 days — a proposed refinement, not tested in the paper. Horizon studied: Portfolios formed monthly on the filing. Sources: Supports — Cohen, Malloy & Pomorski (2012), Journal of Finance 67(3) (Corporate insiders, 1986–2007), www.nber.org/papers/w16454 ↗.

signalsCongressColumnHtml:
The Congress column on the Institutional tab

Every row of the Named moves and every Consensus row on /signals counts the members of Congress who traded the same name, on the same side, inside the 13F quarter. It is a co-occurrence in public filings — never coordination, never intent.

  • Quarter. The 13F period must be a calendar quarter end (March 31, June 30, September 30 or December 31); otherwise no line is joined and the tab says so. The Congress window is that quarter by trade date, inclusive: the first day of its first month through the quarter end. Filed dates are not bounded: every line the build knows counts.
  • Lines. Rows without a date anomaly, traded inside the quarter, a listed stock as filed (the House Clerk's ST or the Senate's Stock — never inferred from an asset's name), with a ticker, on a purchase or a sale; a partial sale counts as a sale. Exchanges and unparsed sides are left out.
  • Sides. A new stake or an add is matched with purchases; a trim or an exit with sales. A Consensus row and the Consensus card count both sides.
  • Tickers. Compared in the SEC spelling (upper case, "." read as "-"), so BRK.B meets BRK-B, while GOOG and GOOGL stay distinct. A 13F name that no reviewed ticker maps joins nothing, and says so.
  • Members. Each counted once, by congressional identifier, or by the filed name when none is on record.
  • Broad accounts. A member who traded more than 25 distinct tickers in the quarter matches almost any name, so the column does not count them; its tip names each one with that count. Where only broad accounts traded a name, the row, its opened body, the Consensus row, the Consensus card and the name's detail say so — never "none" — and name them; they are still not counted.
  • Detail. An opened row lists at most 12 lines per side, each with its range, both dates and its receipt; the rest are on the ticker page.
